item.title: The hypersonic missile race is an unnecessary boondoggle for US
item.description:
Last year, a group of high-ranking former military personnel and weapons company executives issued an ominous warning in an Atlantic Council report. U.S. adversaries, they said, were making rapid advances in hypersonic missile technology, “posing a severe challenge to US battlefield dominance.”

“Now is the time to act decisively to close the hypersonic gap and defend the nation’s interests for the future,” the report declared.

But is this really an existential threat? Will these technologies be as truly groundbreaking as the defense-tech industry claims? Experts who spoke with RS cast doubt on these positions, arguing that the spending is wasteful because despite the hype, hypersonics won’t provide unique advantages for the United States.

Hypersonic missiles can reach speeds of over Mach 5 and remain maneuverable mid-flight to confuse defensive systems. The missiles are designed to evade traditional ballistic missile defense systems by flying at low altitude, leaving them difficult to detect until minutes or even seconds before striking a target. In comparison, traditional ballistics follow high, extraatmospheric, parabolic arcs, allowing radar systems to detect them before they reach their zenith, sometimes affording defenders more than 20 minutes of warning before impact.

Claims about the difficulty of intercepting hypersonics aren’t airtight. Despite successful tests of some hypersonics, some experts doubt the feasibility of the claimed maximum speeds, maneuverability, and stealth abilities, according to Scientific American. The Congressional Budget Office agrees, insisting that “technological challenges must still be overcome to field hypersonic missiles.” According to the CBO, if fielded, the weapons would cost at least 30% more per unit than their ballistic counterparts. Even then, they would be more useful than ballistics only against extremely advanced, long-range defense systems, which no US adversaries currently possess.

Still, claims of successful tests or deployments of hypersonics by Russia, China, North Korea, and Iran have caused concern in the national security establishment about growing risks to Washington’s aerial dominance and, particularly, the ability of these weapons to get past U.S. missile defense systems. As of October 2026, Russia has reportedly tested two maneuvering hypersonic systems, and it has used regular hypersonic missiles (Oreshnik) in the war against Ukraine.

Iran and North Korea’s claims of hypersonic capabilities remain unverified by independent observers. China has a confirmed hypersonic weapon, with unconfirmed reports suggesting additional successes.

The chase for hypersonics ignores a larger geopolitical context, says Kelly Greico of the Stimson Center , who argues the United States’ major adversaries are acting out of a sense of vulnerability rather than a desire for escalation. For Russia and China, this stems from the transfer of U.S. THAAD (Terminal High Altitude Area Defense) missile defense systems into Ukraine and South Korea. U.S. adversaries see these batteries as giving cover to U.S. activities in their respective regions, making it easier for the U.S. to attack without having to worry too much about defending its equipment and personnel in the region. If hypersonics can evade such defenses, these countries can theoretically respond effectively to any American incursions in the region, thus acting as a deterrent.

In this context, these advanced, but expensive and rare, munitions make strategic sense. For a country like Iran, which can manufacture missiles more cheaply and has more limited resources, investing in a few highly advanced long-range missiles to increase deterrence in a future conflict makes strategic sense. In hypothetical wars — and indeed, in the ongoing war in the Persian Gulf — Iran is defending itself close to home against a militarily superior enemy. A country like Iran or China knows that even the threat of a strike to key U.S. sites, or even against the American homeland, would be intolerable for the U.S. and perhaps prevent an attack.

However, Greico felt that, given expensive military supply chains, a less developed missile manufacturing sector, and a different overall strategic orientation, these munitions would do little to enhance American security. The U.S. typically aims to maintain aerial superiority to carry out offensive strikes against an enemy with comparably minimal aerial defenses. Greico says existing, cheaper ballistic missiles launched en masse would be just as effective at evading or overwhelming any countermeasures. Additionally, she believes the United States’ nuclear triad already serves as a more than effective nuclear deterrent that wouldn’t be improved by hypersonic development.

Yet the U.S. is moving ahead with large-scale hypersonics development. Recently, the Pentagon offered private industry incentives to help close the alleged gap, with procurement contracts totaling over $12 billion for FY 2027. This staggering sum excludes additional research and development spending. Although traditional players like Boeing, Lockheed Martin, and Northrop Grumman are in the mix, defense-tech startups are also trying their hand. Pentagon procurement overhauls in 2025 changed the rules to benefit younger, more innovative companies. Since then, venture capital investment in the hypersonic sector has more than tripled, rising to $1.2 billion in 2025 from $220 million the year prior.

Newcomer Castelion demonstrates this trend well. As of September 2026, the company is valued at $14 billion after raising $1 billion in Series C funding, largely from venture capital, and winning nearly $500 million in Defense Department contracts this year alone. In September 2026, the Navy placed a nearly $44 million order for 444 rounds of the Castellion hypersonic strike missile, known as the Blackbeard, making it one of its largest such contracts to date.

Greico advised caution toward large-scale investment in immature technologies like hypersonics.

Pointing to a Government Accountability Office (GAO) report, Greico said the projects are already behind schedule. The GAO reported in July that the Army and Navy alone have already approved over $50 billion in investments and procurement of hypersonic missile technologies. As of July, the Navy Conventional Prompt Strike (CPS) Program is 24 months behind on modifying ships to carry the $50 million-a-piece CPS missiles. The Dark Eagle, a missile developed jointly by the Army and Navy that will serve as the backbone of the Army’s hypersonic arsenal, is already delayed by two years.

There is no central strategy for hypersonic investment. Julia Gledhill, a researcher and defense budgetary expert at the Stimson Center, explained there is no easy way to get a single number for the total U.S. investment in hypersonics today. “You have hypersonic funding in Golden Dome, in the Defense Production Act Money that is focused on industrial base expansion,” she said, adding that they were on the new Pentagon Munitions Acceleration Council’s list of 12 critical munitions.

Greico and Gledhill both said any strategic gains from hypersonics would be marginal at best and that greater investment risked entering a costly escalatory spending cycle with countries like Russia and China, as each strives to gain a technological upper hand with increasingly complex counter systems. Gledhill pointed to Trump’s “Golden Dome for America” as an example, comparing it to the ill-fated Reagan-era “Star Wars” initiative. Estimated to cost at least $1.2 trillion over 20 years, the program aims to build an orbital nuclear missile defense system. Scientists have already dubbed it a “fantasy,” and experts say it would be an unprecedented escalation in militarizing space.

Greico offered a simple explanation for why Washington is continuing this pursuit despite its myriad challenges. Hypersonic investment is “a culture thing,” she said. “There seems to be discomfort with being behind.”

item.title: Time for a harsh truth: even with Netanyahu gone, the killing won’t stop in Gaza | Owen Jones
item.description:
It’s naive to think the Israeli opposition will act very differently. Look at what it has said about even the most vulnerable Palestinians

“Every child, every baby in Gaza is the enemy.” In a normal society, a politician who said something so depraved would face total reputational ruin. Not so in Israel. Meet Moshe Feiglin, previously considered a “far-right outcast”, who has just been elected to Israel’s legislature. He said this last May, but he has also called for more Palestinian babies to die and for Gaza’s entire population, newborns included, to be expelled. In last month’s election, Feiglin formed an alliance with Bezalel Smotrich, the far-right finance minister. Benjamin Netanyahu welcomed this “important union” and praised their “national responsibility”.

Feiglin’s words are not simply the ravings of an extremist politician. Israel has waged what Save the Children describes as a “war on children”. A UN independent commission concluded earlier this year that Israeli forces had deliberately targeted and killed Palestinian children. According to figures from the Palestinian ministry of health – which are likely significant underestimates – nearly 22,000 children in Gaza have been killed since Israel began its assault, including at least 1,100 under the age of one.

What do you call a ceasefire when the firing has not ceased? The killings in Gaza decreased when the truce was announced last October, but they did not end. Israel’s strike on Thursday morning on one of the few remaining functioning hospitals, which killed six people and wounded 28 more, was the first on a healthcare facility since then. But it was not an anomaly. About four Palestinians a day have died on average since the ceasefire was declared.

The Israeli military said that it had struck a Hamas commander and other fighters in the attack on Nasser hospital, without providing evidence. Its record does not inspire confidence in the accuracy of its account. Multiple UN experts and health campaigners have warned of the deliberate targeting of medical facilities and healthcare workers. item.description:
Welcome to The Iron Triangle, the Cipher Brief column serving Procurement Officers tasked with buying the future, Investors funding the next generation of defense technology, and the Policy Wonks analyzing its impact on the global order.

In the industrial parks of Guangdong, the hardest part of the drone war is the visitor schedule. Ukrainian drone makers who travel to their Chinese component suppliers describe hosts who choreograph visits so that Ukrainian and Russian buyers never share a building. Separate doors. Service corridors. Empty conference rooms. Oleksandr Yakovenko, founder of TAF Industries, one of Ukraine's largest drone producers, told the Financial Times that his suppliers "try to make it so we will not be in the same factory at the same time." By the paper's account, the car carrying the Russians pulls out and the car carrying the Ukrainians pulls in.

That is not a supplier. That is a referee. And this month the referee is rewriting the rules.

The Valve

On October 19, Beijing published Announcement No. 49, revising dual-use export controls on 13 categories of drone components and technology, effective November 18. It reaches heavy multirotor motors and speed controllers, long-range autopilots, inertial navigation, datalinks, and engines. Read the signature block before the parts list: the notice was issued by the Ministry of Commerce, the General Administration of Customs, and the Equipment Development Department of the Central Military Commission. The military's equipment office co-signed Beijing's drone controls in 2023 too. This was never trade policy.

The design matters more than the scope. Announcement 49 bans nothing. It requires licenses, and licensing allows treatment to differ by exporter, destination, and end user. A ban is a wall. A license is a valve, and Beijing keeps its hand on it.

The second date resolved itself the day this column went to the editor, and the way it resolved is the point. China's suspension of its sweeping October 2025 rare earth controls, the ones that reach any foreign product containing as little as 0.1 percent Chinese-origin rare earth by value, was due to lapse on November 10. For six weeks the diplomacy said January while the legal notice said November. On November 9, with one day to spare, Beijing extended the pause to January 10. Two months. Nothing closed, and every magnet buyer in the West spent the autumn planning for a license queue anyway. A valve does not have to turn to work. It only has to be seen in someone's hand.

Three Wars, One Parts Bin

Start with what these parts do. By the Financial Times's count, drones account for up to three quarters of recent losses in Ukraine. The parts bin is where the killing power comes from.

Moscow. China's share of Russia's imports of the goods the G7 flags as battlefield priorities rose from 54.3 percent in 2022 to 84.6 percent in 2025. Russia does not have a supply chain. It has a supplier.

Kyiv. Ukraine has worked to get out. At the start of 2024, nearly 90 percent of its imported drone components came directly from China. In the first eight months of 2026, the figure was 28 percent. The number flatters. Some of the parts arriving through Poland and the Czech Republic were most likely made in China too, and Yakovenko told the Associated Press that switching entirely to Western parts could raise costs by as much as 60 percent and cut production by about the same. Andrii Taganskyi, whose company Odd Systems builds drone cameras, summed up the rest: "Without this 5%, there is no camera."

Then there is the detail that should keep Brussels up at night. In July, the EU let Kyiv spend part of a €5.9 billion drone tranche of its defense loan on Chinese components, because Europe cannot make enough of them. That loan is money Europe borrowed on the capital markets, to be repaid if Russia ever pays reparations. So European debt, backed by a Russian IOU, buys Chinese parts for Ukrainian drones, from the same supplier base arming Russia. Nobody planned that, but everybody signed it.

Taipei, by way of Washington. If you think the valve only turns for Europe's war, ask Skydio. In October 2024, Beijing sanctioned America's largest drone maker after Washington approved defense assistance for Taiwan. Chinese authorities visited Skydio's suppliers, including a TDK battery subsidiary in Dongguan, and told them to stop. Skydio rationed batteries to one per drone. Its only customer in Taiwan, the company pointed out, was the National Fire Agency. Its customer in Ukraine had ordered thousands of drones. A decision about Taiwan became battery rationing at the company supplying Ukraine. One parts bin, three wars.

The Wall We Built

Washington's answer has been prohibitions. On January 1, the DFARS magnet restriction expands to bar contractors from delivering neodymium-iron-boron and samarium-cobalt magnets if any step in the chain, from mining through refining, melting, and finished production, takes place in a covered country. Since September 3, Proclamation 11055 has imposed Section 232 duties of 10 to 100 percent on imported drones and components.

Each measure is defensible. Together they make a wall with very little stacked behind it. On June 30, the Army opened its first domestic small-drone motor line at Tobyhanna Army Depot, 1,500 motors a day. Adamas Intelligence, which tracks the magnet trade, reports that the magnets inside those motors are still roughly 90 percent Chinese-made. The Pentagon knows it. In May, the Defense Logistics Agency placed $25.8 million in sole-source orders with two U.S.-based magnet makers and paid $2 million to qualify a third. Set $25.8 million beside a program buying drones by the hundred thousand. The magnet rule has exceptions, including one for commercial off-the-shelf items, and they will be used, because the alternative is an idle motor line. A wall you have to keep waiving is not a wall. This is not a scandal. It is a feature of buying the airframe and hoping the bill of materials sorts itself out.

The tariff has its own irony. Taiwan, the democracy building a "non-red" drone supply chain as national policy, is slated to pay a reduced but real 15 percent combined rate on its drones. We are taxing the exit.

For the Procurement Officer

The Drone Dominance Program wants more than 200,000 one-way attack drones. Call it 800,000 motors. Chinese brushless motors have sold for $12 to $25 against $100 to $225 for American equivalents. Those were smaller motors at last year's prices, so treat the result as an order of magnitude: the premium to buy every one of those motors outside China lands somewhere around $60 to $170 million. The program is worth $1.1 billion. Independence for the most exposed component costs less than a rounding error on Golden Dome. You are not short of money. You are short of a contract that buys components instead of airframes.

The Investment Thesis

The bottleneck premium is moving down the bill of materials. Airframe makers are plentiful; hundreds applied to fly the Gauntlet. Magnet makers, motor winders, and camera-sensor houses that can document a clean chain back to the mine are not. On January 1, the documentation becomes the product. Price accordingly.

The Policy Wonk's Warning

Beijing has built the only arms-control regime of the drone age that is actually effective. No treaty, no verification, no Senate ratification. Just a licensing desk that can decide, case by case, whose drones fly in Ukraine. It has already used that desk to punish a Taiwan decision. Assume it will do so again when the Strait gets tense, and that the first sign will be paperwork, not ships.

My Take.

We do not need a wall. We need our own valve, and building one takes three moves.

First, pool demand. Washington's Drone Dominance money and Europe's Ukraine loan should buy components, not just finished drones, on multi-year offtake contracts that a magnet plant can take to a bank.

Second, write one list. Taiwan's ITRI is already the only overseas certifier in the U.S.-led Green UAS program. On October 27, at a forum in Taipei co-hosted by Taiwan's foreign ministry, John Hemmings of the Henry Jackson Society proposed that Taiwan and Europe agree on a red-free standard, certify suppliers, and stand up a drone supply chain office to write the testing rules. Fold Ukraine in, add the United States, and make it one certified-supplier list across the alliance.

Third, make the list worth something. Certified allied components should enter at zero duty. The proclamation already carves out zero-rate lanes for approved onshoring plans. Extend that logic to allies who are onshoring for all of us.

That is how a parts bin becomes an alliance.

The Risk.

The valve leaks. Ukrainian firms keep finding ways around Chinese restrictions through intermediaries, and Chinese factories have little appetite for losing a customer that size. Announcement 49 also aims high: standard five- and seven-inch FPVs fall below its motor thresholds, while heavy-lift and long-range systems take the hit. A fair reader could say Beijing is managing a market, not picking a winner. My answer is the last six weeks. Beijing closed nothing, and the West planned around it anyway. A regime that can be precise is more dangerous than one that is blunt, because it can squeeze one end user without disturbing anyone else's quarterly numbers.

Conclusion

Somewhere in Shenzhen this week, a sales manager is timing the cars in the parking lot so that two warring delegations never meet. America has already had its visit. In 2024 the men who came to the factory were Chinese officials, and the customer they cut off was ours. If Beijing can already decide which side's drones fly over Ukraine, what makes us so confident it will not decide whose fly over the Strait?

item.title: Iran Is Poking The Bear
item.description:
Tehran has been playing a dangerous game of chicken with the U.S. administration for months. With the just concluded midterms now in hand, they risk making a dangerous miscalculation just when it matters most. This is unlikely to end well.

With the continuation of strikes this week against international shipping transiting the Strait of Hormuz, while simultaneously engaging in renewed negotiations, Tehran is poking the bear with one hand while feeding it with the other. This is a dangerous strategy; they could lose a hand… or worse.

The Iranian leadership is clearly trying to have it both ways. Equal parts emboldened and wary, with a hefty dose of economic reality rapidly bearing down upon them.

Tehran is and always has been a keen observer of American politics. This time, however, they appear to be overconfident, and potentially risk acting on a tragic misreading of the situation. This two-pronged strategy - continued taunting, both verbal and military, while offering to negotiate, sort of – appears to indicate they perceive a deep new vulnerability in their opponent given the historic drubbing the administration received in the midterms. That is possible, and the administration will certainly face harsh scrutiny over its handling of the war. But it is also possible that they are seeing a President Trump who is merely stunned and, if such a thing is possible… humbled, if only for the moment. But this humility is unlikely to last. The President retains primary control over U.S. foreign and military policy, and there are already reports of plans for massive new strikes if negotiations again fail, or the President becomes frustrated with Tehran’s usual stalling and stubbornness.

The President is already looking for a fall-guy within his administration for a failed, unpopular war, and the devastating impact on the midterms; with the odds-on favorite(s) being Secretary of Defense Hegseth and/or senior military leaders. He is almost certain to look for one outside his administration as well, with Iran the certain candidate for their unwillingness to accede to the President’s attempts at diplomacy pre-election. He has proven that he is nothing if not vengeful. At the same time, the President wants a deal and appears ready for one. Unless, that is, Tehran insists on rubbing his face in a less than optimal resolution. This risks a reaction that would serve no one.

Tehran’s hubris is legend. As is that of President Trump. When these meet head-to-head – hubris to hubris – the result is at best uncertain, and potentially disastrous.

In the end, the most likely conclusion remains a negotiated settlement. Iran has several advantages, including geography, proven resilience and staying power. And their just-concluded conclave with Russia is a new, ominous development that bodes ill. On the other hand, the U.S. administration may finally have an effective strategy in its naval/economic blockade. But this will take time, and it may no longer have the political runway to see it through.

Tehran should declare victory and allow the U.S. President to go home. Face-saving measures are essential for both sides to avoid the additional death and destruction that is sure to follow military escalation, by either side.

But this will not be the final bell. Tehran will be left to its own devices to face the enormous challenges of a shattered economy, a degraded environment, and a restive population.

This is not over by a long shot.

I am reposting portions of a previous post given their continued relevance

Iran Is “Counting Coup” On The United States!

“Iran is playing a very dangerous game. In the face of the awesome military power of the United States, in between desultory negotiating sessions, they continue to touch the enemy by launching attacks against U.S. and allied Gulf facilities. Recently, they have reached farther afield, striking U.S. assets in an Egyptian port. This would seem to be inexplicable behavior, given the U.S.’s obvious desire for a deal, inviting as it has strong retaliatory strikes against Iran’s increasingly beleaguered military, and potentially civilian, infrastructure. Most recently, we are seeing reports of possible Iranian cyberattacks on the water supplies of U.S. cities; such activities are certain to continue and likely to escalate, plausibly deniable and effective in sowing fear as they are. The question is why?”

“It may be simple hubris. It may be a misread of the desperation of their opponent. Or simply overconfidence in the strength of their position. It most certainly is part and parcel of a purposeful negotiating strategy, a reminder to all involved that Iranian forces can reach out and touch you whenever they wish.

Regardless, they are walking a fine line, and they have placed this conflict squarely in the crosshairs of unintended consequences.

As they so often do, they risk overreaching. Should one of these missile or drone strikes make it through, whether by luck or skill, and inflict truly significant casualties on U.S. personnel, either in a land-based facility or on a naval vessel for example, this could surge American support for a massive response, possibly including – however unlikely – ground troops, radically altering and escalating the course of this conflict.”

“The Iranian leadership’s actions, however, are likely aimed not only at the United States but may be the result of continued factional maneuvering in Tehran, as groups jockey for advantage for what comes next. Now that it appears likely the regime will survive, they are no doubt looking ahead to where they will land in a new regime. As both factions and individuals.”

As I wrote in ‘Is Iran Controlling the Gulf Conflict?’: “I would posit that the newly ascended Supreme Leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, may in fact be a phantom leader. Alive in some fashion, perhaps largely incapacitated, but not actually in charge. And even if able to coherently express his views, in no way nearly as powerful or influential as his father. The seemingly reckless actions of the regime in courting U.S. retaliation may in actuality reflect a lack of a coherent decision-making process as opposed to a unified one. I think it is quite possible that competing factions within the regime are using Mojtaba as an avatar while they maneuver for decisive advantage.”

On 15 May, I laid out in “Ground Hog Day”, a recommended way forward for the U.S. that I think largely still applies. It is a measure of how fruitless continued military action is that these remain relevant today:

“Make a deal with Iran. One that they will accept. This will require painful concessions and is certain to include provisions that many will find objectionable, including significant sanctions relief. And it will leave the Iranian regime in place and in control of Iran. For now.”

“As much as I would prefer to see regime change in Iran, I believe a deal may be the only realistic way out of the Groundhog Day-like doom loop in which we find ourselves. Simply put, the administration squandered the initial opportunity presented by a unique confluence of events by its lack of strategic planning and a fundamental misunderstanding of Iran and the Iranian regime.”

“As a result, we are going to have to step back and take a longer view. I pity the people of Iran, at least in the near term. They are certain to suffer the brunt of the regime’s immediate ire. That is a hard truth.”

“This is not, however, the end of the story. Iran’s internal weaknesses still matter–and may shape what comes next more than battlefield successes. I am cautiously, very cautiously optimistic that even barring regime change, Iran’s leadership will be forced to change direction.”

“The issues facing Iran prior to the War were serious, in fact existential – a collapsing economy, hyper-inflation, severe water shortages, lack of electricity, and growing widespread popular anger and unrest – and are ongoing and only getting worse. Whatever the Iranian leadership looks like, it will have to address these issues. And it is not clear that they will be capable of doing this without outside help. This is where the U.S. and hopefully our Western allies come in: sanctions relief, and extensive economic and other assistance in exchange for real changes in policy and a pullback on objectionable activities and programs. The potential for this may, and I say may, have increased with the removal of Ali Khamenei from the Supreme Leader’s seat. But it will depend on whether his son and successor, Mojtaba, is less rigidly ideological than his father. We will see if he is willing to put the Iranian people ahead of the regime.”

It is becoming more obvious by the day that the U.S. needs to come to a negotiated settlement with Iran. And the terms of this settlement are certain to be painful and unsatisfactory from the perspective of the West. But continuing tit-for-tat airstrikes simply prolongs the pain and risks horrific unintended consequences without solving the problem, as well as providing the regime with a distraction from its appalling management of Iran’s economy, natural resources, and foreign policy.

An enraged and restive Iranian population awaits. Let the regime face, without fear or favor, the fruits of its mismanagement, leaving it to confront what it fears most: the streets. This is likely where genuine regime change will occur.

item.title: Squabble over leadership risks plunging the OSCE into crisis
item.description:
The Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) is staring down the barrel of entering 2027 without a chair for the first time in its 51-year history.

The Europeans are wrestling Turkey to drop its veto over Cyprus’ bid, raising the stakes by loudly opposing the only other candidate, Georgia. Unable to win over Ankara, Europe should drop its objections to Tbilisi to avert a crisis.

With three weeks to go until the OSCE Ministerial Council in Lugano, Switzerland, on December 3, the organization remains deadlocked over who should lead it from 2027-28. The chairperson-in-office role rotates every two years and is normally voted on well in advance with agreement by consensus. EU member Cyprus was the first country to put its hat in the ring almost two years ago, in December 2024.

However, Cyprus’ bid has been vetoed by Turkey on the basis of the long-standing dispute over the division of the island in 1974. There is a long history of enmity over the issue between NATO members Turkey and Greece, the latter of which has long backed Cyprus and opposed Turkey’s occupation of half of the island. Indeed, each country has vetoed the other across numerous areas of dialogue and cooperation. Just this past week, the Hellenic American Leadership Council (HALC) began lobbying the Trump Administration to veto Turkey’s candidate to become U.N. secretary general.

With this history in mind, it’s clear, at least to me, that the Turkish are never going to back down over Cyprus’ candidature for the OSCE chair role.

That leaves a second candidate, Georgia, which entered the race in January. However, in late September 2026, 14 European countries came out to block Tbilisi, without raising specific objections. This does not represent a veto. Instead, the EU has said that it will not consider other candidates apart from Cyprus, in an election that requires consensus.

Refusing to consider Georgia has resulted in the current stalemate. Europe is effectively taking the chairmanship to the wire, in a bid to force through Cyprus’ candidate. It’s not going to work.

This fight raises the real prospect of the OSCE entering 2027 without a chair, leaving it unable, for the first time, to agree on leadership, budgets or meaningful action on the core security priorities of its region, including on Ukraine.

The organization comprises 57 member states, including the United States, Russia, and most of Europe and Central Asia. A headless OSCE would cripple the only remaining body in Europe that exists to promote dialogue between countries in times of conflict. This at a time when European states have sidelined bilateral diplomacy with Russia because of the Ukraine war, such that the Europeans have been left out of last week’s Abu Dhabi peace talks.

With the unstoppable Europeans facing off against the immovable Turks, the obvious solution would be to drop objections to Georgia’s candidacy.

There are strong arguments in favor of Georgia. It straddles one of the hottest geopolitical crossroads in the world, with Russia to its north and Iran to its south. Turkey, while generally on good terms with Tbilisi, has a deeply troubled relationship with Armenia.

The fraught geopolitical tightrope that Georgia has had to tread on Russia is precisely why it would make a good chair of the OSCE. Indeed, Georgia assumed the chair of the OSCE’s Forum for Security Cooperation in April of this year — and with none of the attending drama.

The current government of Georgia has delivered an impressive track record of economic growth and reform that suggests it has the institutional credentials and credibility to lead. It remains a country committed to future membership in the EU despite the difficulties in the relationship, as the prime minister set out at the recent EU Enlargement Summit.

This last-minute European barrier to Georgia’s candidacy appears in part linked to the deterioration in Georgian-European relations since the start of the war in Ukraine in 2022. While the Georgian government has consistently and repeatedly backed Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity in official statements, it has found itself in the European crosshairs for not joining economic sanctions against Russia or getting involved with the war effort.

The reasons for this are pragmatic. Georgia suffered a brief yet devastating war against Russia in 2008 and the loss of a significant chunk of its territory in Abkhazia and South Ossetia. Having visited Georgia often over the past two years, it is clear to me that the loss of territory to Russia represents a deep scar that runs through Georgian society irrespective of which political party citizens support.

The idea that Georgia is a Russian ally because it refuses to expose itself to the risk of another damaging war is frankly ludicrous. Georgia still does not maintain diplomatic relations with Russia. Its careful positioning on the war has occasionally put it at odds with the government of Ukraine. And yet Ukraine is not opposing Georgia’s OSCE bid. Nor are the United States, Canada, Russia, Georgia’s immediate neighbours or the Central Asian participating states.

Georgia has faced criticism from Europe for clamping down on foreign-funded NGOs. Some Western commentators argue that U.S. and European lawmakers want to deliver a Maidan-style revolution in Georgia.

However, these disagreements are entirely incidental to the issue of Georgia’s candidacy to chair the OSCE. The organization was first founded in 1975 (initially as the CSCE) as part of the Helsinki Final Act to facilitate greater dialogue on security between western Europe, the Soviet Union and the Warsaw Pact. It has always been, purposefully, a big tent that even today can accommodate Russia and Ukraine, Armenia and Azerbaijan, Turkey and Cyprus, Kosovo and Serbia, and so on.

It was perhaps inevitable at some point that a party to a frozen conflict within the group would one day step forward to assume the chairman role, prompting a veto from the other party. This is exactly what has happened with Cyprus’ candidature, which has become an immovable blockage with Europe and Turkey unwilling to give ground.

The EU is never going to win that fight, which leaves the OSCE deadlocked with mere weeks to run.

So, the Europeans are in the invidious position of not being able to force through their own candidate for the chairman role while blocking the only other credible candidate, Georgia, on procedural grounds. This is deeply unhelpful in circumstances where neither Ukraine nor Russia see objections to Georgia assuming the role.

If the OSCE enters a new year without a chair, the OSCE will have become a reflection of Europe’s divisions rather than a mechanism for managing them. It’s time for European nations to drop their objections to Georgia’s candidacy and avoid plunging the OSCE into 2027 in a state of crisis.

item.title: The UK and the EU need an economic security partnership
item.description:
The UK and the EU need an economic security partnership Expert comment thilton.drupal 16 November 2026

The UK–EU Summit is an opportunity to secure a new partnership suitable for an increasingly hostile global economy. It should start with an information-sharing arrangement about high-risk investments, including from China.

The second UK–EU ‘reset’ summit takes place on 20 November, after a six-month delay to give prime minister Andy Burnham’s new government time to settle in and set its priorities. 

It is expected to deliver on the deals kickstarted by the Starmer government, most of which focus on reducing barriers to trade and mobility. These include a sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) agreement that removes most checks on trade in animals, plants, and their products, as well as a youth experience scheme and the linking of the UK and EU emissions trading systems. Completing these agreements is important for growth – the UK government estimates the SPS deal could eventually be worth £5.1 billion a year – and for building trust with the EU after years of political setbacks.

But the Burnham government will likely also want a more strategic partnership with the EU on security, defence and geopolitics. Central to this should be the goal of economic security, which has become a key priority for governments around the world. Economic security revolves around protecting sensitive national assets from hostile interference or exploitation, withstanding coercion and supply shocks, and building the strategic capabilities needed to stay competitive.

Beyond ‘Made in Europe’

Much of the reporting on this topic has focused on whether UK firms will be covered by the EU’s ‘Made in Europe’ initiatives. These measures – the most significant of which are in the proposed Industrial Accelerator Act – favour European-made products in public procurement and subsidy schemes, with the aim of rebuilding the EU’s industrial base and reducing its strategic dependencies. The concern is that, unless UK-made goods are treated the same as European-made ones, these initiatives risk shutting UK firms out of European supply chains.

Related work

Brussels or Beijing? The EU’s ‘Made in Europe’ plans will force the UK to choose 

For now, the decision over ‘Made in Europe’ appears to have been kicked into next year. But ‘Made in Europe’ is only one part of the picture, albeit a critical one. Since Brexit, the global economy has become far more adversarial. The US is more willing to use tariffs as bargaining chips, while China is restricting exports of critical inputs such as rare earths to advance its geopolitical goals. 

In a forthcoming paper, we argue that middle powers such as the UK need to work together to manage these pressures. Partners like Australia, Canada, Japan and South Korea will be critical. But the EU is the UK’s most consequential economic security partner, due to its proximity, integrated supply chains and shared security interests. The UK’s approach to the upcoming summit should therefore put economic security cooperation as a crucial pillar of the reset in UK–EU relations.

Economic security partnership

The UK and the EU share challenges ranging from coercion and Chinese overcapacity to an unpredictable US. They also have shared dependencies in critical minerals, energy and some advanced technologies. 

A new UK–EU economic security partnership would give both sides a regular, structured mechanism to share information and coordinate on these risks. 

This partnership could build on existing structures. These could include the Partnership Council set up in 2021 under the Trade and Cooperation Agreement, the 2025 Security and Defence Partnership, and the annual UK–EU summits. The partnership would also involve designated channels being established across each government to coordinate information-sharing and policy objectives as part of its structure. 

As part of this partnership, the EU and the UK should initiate an annual ministerial dialogue on economic security, supported by official-level working groups. This would compare assessments of geo-economic risks, including from China, and discuss approaches to coercion, industrial policy and overcapacity. It should also consider ways to jointly engage other like-minded partners on trade norms and to address geo-economic shocks, such as the energy price crisis that followed the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

From the outset, the partnership should also include a commitment to consult on how to respond if either side faces retaliation for measures taken together. This could apply if the UK were to align with EU tariffs or investment conditions on Chinese goods or capital, for example as part of securing ‘Made in Europe’ treatment. In this scenario, the UK should act within an agreed process for managing any consequences. That would give both sides a framework within which to negotiate how to align their economic security.

Start with protective tools

Aligning tariffs and industrial policy is politically and economically challenging. This is partly because the UK and the EU compete in certain industrial sectors and for investment. It’s also because the UK sits outside the trading bloc and cannot currently benefit from the EU’s single market or the Anti-Coercion Instrument (nicknamed the ‘trade bazooka’), its new trade tool aimed at deterring and responding to economic coercion. 

Rather than initially seeking this alignment, the partnership should therefore instead begin by strengthening cooperation to address the risks posed by hostile actors acquiring or accessing sensitive assets. These include data, technology and intellectual property.

Related work

China and its trading partners are moving towards an economic peace. But it is a fragile one

At present, the UK and the EU share too little information on investment risks, research security and vulnerabilities in critical supply chains. Closer cooperation in these areas carries lower political and economic costs than aligning on tariffs. And it plays to the UK’s strengths. 

The UK’s National Security and Investment Act (NSIA) is one of the more developed screening regimes in Europe, while the EU only recently made it mandatory for all member states to screen investments for national security risks. A practical first step would be an information-sharing arrangement between the UK’s Investment Security Unit and EU member states’ screening authorities. This would also help address concerns on both sides about high-risk investments, including those from China. 

Over time, this would make it easier to share sensitive technology, capital and research. It would help build the trust needed for harder decisions on industrial policy and trade defence. 

A more ambitious agenda

Once that trust is established, the partnership should pursue a more ambitious agenda. First, this should build on the information-sharing set out above to establish a joint early warning arrangement for supply-chain disruption as soon as possible, modelled on the aims of the US-Japan-South Korea system, connecting the UK’s Supply Chain Centre with the EU’s monitoring of critical goods. 

Over the next two years, it should also include a channel for coordinating responses to coercion, including how the UK’s emerging anti-coercion framework could work alongside the EU’s Anti-Coercion Instrument. And it should foster strategic industrial collaboration over the long term, including pooling resources and talent. 

However, while political will is growing on both sides, cooperation on economic security still faces challenges. The EU is wary of extending subsidy and procurement benefits without commitments that ensure reciprocal access to UK schemes and alignment on tariffs and investment conditions towards China. For its part, the UK will resist overt rule-taking or limits on its freedom to set its own trade policy. 

The best way to begin addressing some of these challenges is to start with information-sharing, which asks less of either side than full alignment. It would start to answer EU concerns about Chinese investment and build the trust both sides need for harder decisions later. 

The effort is worth it. Despite Brexit, the UK’s long-term economic future ultimately remains closely tied to Europe’s. 

This is particularly true when it comes to shared economic security. A forward-looking UK–EU economic security partnership would help protect both economies from coercion and supply shocks, strengthening the industries that both will depend on while navigating an increasingly hostile global economy.

item.description:
The downfall of the Israeli PM may seem inevitable now; it is anything but. He must be ejected from office and brought to justice

It’s unsporting to kick a man when he’s down. But let’s make an exception for Benjamin Netanyahu. Ever since his far-right coalition government lost its mandate in last month’s national elections, Israel’s prime minister has been making an ugly spectacle of himself. His antics resemble those of a condemned man, desperately scrabbling to escape the gallows. This might not matter so much if, as has been widely assumed (and hoped), Netanyahu cannot ultimately avoid the drop. Yet his final downfall remains far from certain.

As protracted, complex talks proceed over who will form Israel’s next administration – certain to be some variety of multiparty coalition – Netanyahu, forced for now into a nominal caretaker role, is going to extraordinary lengths to cling to power, using every dirty trick in his well-thumbed handbook while calling for a “government of national unity” (excluding Arab parties). And the perception he has been hung out to dry by a similarly electorally humbled Donald Trump, his biggest ally, may also prove over-optimistic. Besieged Palestinians in the West Bank and in hungry, flooded Gaza, and the bombed and battered people of Iran, have good reason to be fearful.

Simon Tisdall is a Guardian foreign affairs commentator

The Trump administration has repeatedly threatened Canada with talk of becoming the 51st state. Handing the file to Bessent, Trump announced that the U.S. would use “economic force” to “get rid of that artificially drawn line” between Canada and the United States.

When the Canadian province of Alberta held a referendum on whether they wanted a future referendum on independence, Bessent intervened, saying Alberta would make a perfect partner for the United States. He said Ottawa is frustrating Alberta and its “wealth of natural resources” by not letting it “build a pipeline to the Pacific.” As a solution, he suggested that “we should let them come down into the U.S…. Alberta is a natural partner for the U.S. They have great resources. The Albertans are very independent people." The preliminary referendum was overwhelmingly defeated.

Not wanting boots on the ground in Cuba, Trump turned the Cuba file over to Treasury before the Pentagon. The economic strangulation of Cuba has not toppled the Cuban government, but it has devastated its people. The island is in darkness, and water, food, and medicine are scarce. Tens of thousands of surgeries have been canceled. According to U.N. human rights chief Volker Türk, “children are dying because doctors lack access to essential medical supplies and medicines.”

Employing a strategy of “carrot and stick,” Bessent said sanctions can go up or down depending on the behavior of the Cuban government. The U.N. says Washington’s sanctions are “incompatible with basic principles of international human rights law.” Bessent’s evaluation is that they are working: “It is working in Cuba right now… we are going to bring this regime down.”

Bessent says that, as the strategy is working in Cuba, so it will work in Iran. "Operation Economic Outcast" was supposed to land the killer blow on Iran (and anyone doing business with Iran). And, according to Bessent’s metrics, it did. Even before the war Bessent said, “President Trump ordered… maximum pressure on Iran. And it worked, because in December, their economy collapsed... and this is why the people took to the street.” Bessent told the Senate Banking Committee that “what we have done is created a dollar shortage in the country… The Iranian currency went into free fall, inflation exploded, and hence we have seen the Iranian people out on the street.”

Fast forward to Sunday, Bessant said that the projected 25% contraction of the Iranian economy is “one of the fastest collapses in history” and boasted that “everything I’m doing is working.”

The force of Bessent’s economic war machine received validation from the State Department on November 10, when Rubio assessed that the military war on Iran was no longer necessary because economic war was working better. "The economic pain that is being inflicted on Iran right now is extraordinary,” Rubio told G7 leaders. "We don't need to conduct military strikes if we're achieving the same objective through economic means and economic pressure.” Bessent had been lobbying Trump to take that route.

Of course the Iranians, who after eight months of are still hitting tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and attacking neighbors in the Gulf, like Bahrain, in retaliation for U.S. strikes, might have a word or two to say about that. "Despite all these pressures, the Iranian economy has demonstrated very good resilience, and the claim that Iran’s economy is collapsing is nothing more than an illusion,” Central Bank chief Abdolnaser Hemmati said in October.

The leader of the campaign to negotiate with Iran, meanwhile, has been Vice President JD Vance, who was recently speaking almost every day to Qatari and Pakistani mediators. At the end of October, Vance sent a letter to the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, exploring the possibility of direct talks to stave off the resumption of intense attacks by the U.S.

But two days after Rubio’s endorsement of economic warfare, Trump signed off on it, pulling Vance off the file. Relying on Bessent’s economic approach, Trump said, “we don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”

American foreign policy evolution has in the last 25 years favored the Pentagon and the CIA over the State Department. During the two Trump administrations, as Washington has fully appreciated the power of its dollar dominance and control of trade networks and payment systems, the Treasury has risen to join the two predominant agencies, with Bessent at its helm.

But that doesn’t mean a kinder, gentler form of foreign policy. A landmark study published in The Lancet by Francisco Rodríguez, Silvio Rendón, and Mark Weisbrot found that unilateral U.S. sanctions are associated with death tolls similar to armed conflict. The prevailing weapons may have changed, but the results are all about punishment with very little room for diplomacy or progress toward peace.

item.title: US keeps punishing Iraq to get at Iran
item.description:
Washington’s latest attempt to restrict Iraq’s economic relations with Iran exposes a serious contradiction in the U.S. approach toward Baghdad.

While Washington seeks to establish an expanded bilateral partnership following the withdrawal of its forces from Iraq, it continues to push Baghdad to become part of Washington’s confrontation with Tehran. This policy risks strengthening those political forces in Iraq that Washington seeks to weaken.

On November 8, Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein revealed that the U.S. Treasury had demanded the closure of all but two border crossings with Iran. This in turn followed Trump’s alleged threat to strike Iraqi armed factions if they participated in renewed fighting on behalf of Iran.

Earlier in October, the Treasury imposed sanctions on an Iraqi bank accused of facilitating Iranian sanctions evasion and supporting armed organizations. Earlier measures targeted militia commanders and individuals allegedly exploiting Iraq's oil industry.

But Iran retains an enduring influence in Iraq, a result of both geography and close historical and religious ties. More important is the question of security. Iraq neither can nor wants to serve as Washington’s, or indeed anyone’s, military bulwark against Iran. This thinking has further solidified in Baghdad amid the ongoing war in which Iran has effectively weathered U.S. pressure.

The U.S. has tried to pull Iraq away from Iran under previous Iraqi governments without success. But the latest attempt is driven by the understanding that the current Iraqi prime minister, Ali al-Zaidi, is a politician particularly suited for this kind of mission given his experience as a businessman and his highly transactional approach to foreign policy. Washington also believes that al-Zaidi, as a man hailing from outside the Iraqi political system, would be better able to integrate the Iran-leaning militias into the state.

Yet the problem is that al-Zaidi — having emerged from the Shia Coordination Framework, which includes factions maintaining close relations with Tehran — must balance competing interests while strengthening state institutions. American pressure risks weakening those Iraqi politicians who favor pragmatic cooperation with Washington. Iran-backed factions could portray stringent U.S. demands as evidence that Washington continues to disregard Iraqi sovereignty.

Such arguments may resonate with constituencies that are already critical of decades-long U.S. military operations carried out unilaterally within Iraq’s borders.

Washington appears to believe that disbanding the militias (now postponed by Baghdad to June 2027) would both limit Iran’s influence and benefit Iraq over the longer run. This idea is appealing, but actually carrying it out would not necessarily result in diminishing Tehran’s influence.

Iranian penetration of Iraqi government and society is much greater than just its influence with militias, however powerful they may be. The country’s ministries and other state institutions are packed with bureaucrats and politicians imbued with strong pro-Iranian sentiment. The web of financial and political links between the two countries is such that the notion of “freeing” Iraq from Iran by “disbanding the militias” reflects a fundamental misunderstanding of their relationship.

Limiting Iran’s influence will take a significant amount of time and should ideally go hand in hand with helping create a better investment climate for American and other Western companies. Some moves in this direction have been made. On November 8, Iraqi Deputy Prime Minister for Energy Affairs Mohsen al-Mandalawi met U.S. Chargé d’Affaires Stephen Fagin to discuss implementation of economic agreements worth some $60 billion announced during al-Zaidi's visit to Washington in July.

Promoting closer ties between Iraq on the one hand and Turkey and the Gulf states on the other would also constitute an important step. Syria might not be Iraq’s perfect analogy, but Damascus’ pivot to Turkey and the Gulf states after the fall of the Assad dynasty clearly reduced Iran’s influence there.

Increasing pressure on Iraq over its close ties with Iran at this moment, when U.S. efforts to defeat Iran militarily have clearly fallen short, appears especially ill-timed. The Islamic Republic might be economically highly vulnerable because of Washington’s blockade and tightening sanctions regime, but the country appears to have weathered the external threat. Iran’s neighbors are now more hesitant to pressure the Islamic Republic, which has also managed to reconstitute its military capabilities.

Moreover, Iraq has already suffered substantial economic damage due to disruptions to oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz as a result of the war. On November 8, Hussein estimated Iraq’s losses from the conflict at approximately $60 billion. Although Iraqi oil exports, which account for approximately 90% of government revenue, recovered to around 3.5 million barrels per day in October, compared with 2.65 million in September, the deterioration in government revenues has exposed the country's structural vulnerabilities. Further restrictions on cross-border commerce would impose additional costs on an economy with limited capacity to absorb them.

Economic relations with Iran are also far more extensive than Washington’s demands appear to acknowledge. Bilateral trade reached approximately $12 billion in Iran’s fiscal year ending in March 2025. The Kurdistan region alone reportedly conducts approximately $5 billion in annual trade with Iran. These commercial connections sustain transportation companies, wholesalers, agricultural producers, merchants, and border communities. Their disruption would affect Iraqi businesses whose operations depend on regular cross-border movement.

Moreover, the consequences could extend beyond conventional trade. Iraq has long relied on Iranian natural gas to fuel electricity generation, even as Baghdad has pursued alternative energy supplies. Economic disengagement from Iran is therefore not simply a matter of political willingness. It requires alternative infrastructure, financing, and supply chains that cannot be established overnight.

The Development Road initiative running from Turkey to the Gulf region via Iraqi territory might also serve as an option that would allow Baghdad to lessen dependence on Iran. But the project’s implementation is still in its early stages, and some accommodation with the Iran-aligned militias over ensuring security along the route will be of critical importance to advance the project.

Thus, continued American efforts to constrain Iraq’s regional engagement risk strengthening precisely those political forces that Washington seeks to weaken. Rather than reducing Iranian influence, political pressure could undermine Iraq’s institutions, encourage anti-American mobilization, and diminish Baghdad's willingness to cooperate with Washington on security and economic issues.

item.title: Will Syria entry into Mecca pact mean clash with the Houthis?
item.description:
Syria appears likely to soon join the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, a collective defense agreement established several months ago by Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan. This development would constitute a milestone in Damascus’ efforts to reassert itself within the region’s security architecture following Syria’s gruesome civil war.

Membership in the pact could enhance the legitimacy and prestige of post-Assad Syria while bolstering its military capabilities and deepening partnerships with influential regional states. Syria could benefit from more intelligence cooperation, military training, and Saudi financial support. All this could complement Damascus’ existing security partnership with Ankara.

But it’s not all milk and honey. Joining the security configuration could expose Syria to foreign conflicts and geopolitical rivalries while undermining Damascus’ ability to prioritize redevelopment at home.

There could also be implications for unresolved problems between Syria’s central government and certain minorities. Such frictions stand to exacerbate if Damascus’ entry into the pact leads to rising sectarian temperatures at home and across the region, particularly within the context of Syrian forces being brought into Saudi Arabia’s conflict with Yemen’s Houthi rebels.

Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa will have to weigh these risks carefully as he decides whether to join the bloc.

Security benefits and military implications for Damascus


Syria faces two main threats today. The most immediate one is Israel, which has expanded its illegal occupation of Syrian territory since the former regime’s fall nearly two years ago. Israeli forces have come within 15 miles of Damascus. Since December 2024, Israel has continued launching strikes on Syrian military infrastructure and seeking to empower separatists in the country despite Sharaa offering the Israelis non-aggression and security agreements.

Iran and its “Axis of Resistance” pose the second threat. From Damascus’ perspective, the risk is that Tehran will intensify pressure on Syria to ensure that the Islamic Republic can continue accessing Lebanon for the purpose of arming Hezbollah within the context of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran.

At least on paper, accession to the pact could provide Damascus with another layer of deterrence by increasing potential costs for Tel Aviv and Tehran that would come with future acts of aggression against Syria. But the likelihood that the pact’s signatories would actually intervene militarily on behalf of Damascus is anything but guaranteed.

“Membership of the Mecca Agreement will not immediately allay these pressures in direct security terms,” said James Watt, a former British ambassador who now works for a consultancy called Ambassador Partnership LLP. “But Syria can derive an important degree of confidence from the de facto alliance it has created. In the context of rapid changes in regional security structures, Syria has chosen to join the diplomatic centerpiece of the new regional order. The benefits will amplify over time.”

Syria’s ability to make meaningful contributions to the pact is questionable given the degradation of the country’s armed forces and the immense challenges of rebuilding its military institutions. However, Syria’s combat experiences may prove helpful to Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan.

Indications of a growing Saudi-Syrian security partnership include the reported arrival of Syrian military advisers in Saudi Arabia, Syrian plans to deploy roughly 600 special forces personnel to the kingdom, and the new bilateral defense agreement signed on November 4.

“The only place where [Syria] can contribute to a degree is by providing foot soldiers for the Yemen battle front as it does have battle-hardened, experienced and also ideologically motivated former rebel groups who might be relatively more effective in Yemen as compared to any other external force,” said Umar Karim, an associate fellow at the King Faisal Centre for Research and Islamic Studies, in an RS interview.

However, Watt believes that such a contribution would mostly serve as a gesture of Syrian solidarity with Saudi Arabia in the Saudi-Houthi conflict.

Regardless, any Syrian deployment to the Arabian Peninsula will divert resources away from the country’s dire domestic needs.

Saudi Arabia's growing stake in Syria


As post-Assad Syria’s most important Arab partner, Saudi Arabia would see Damascus’ membership as enhancing Riyadh’s clout in the Levant and strengthening the kingdom’s security partnerships. Damascus joining the pact would further institutionalize Saudi-Syrian ties and enhance efforts to undermine Iran’s ability to reassert itself in Syria.

Noting a “wider Saudi effort to counter Iranian influence beyond the Gulf,” Elijah J. Magnier, a veteran war correspondent and adviser to the European Parliament’s rapporteur on Iraq and Lebanon, explained that “Assad’s fall weakened Tehran’s position in Syria and gave Riyadh an opening.” Furthermore, by “investing in a long-term relationship with Damascus, Saudi Arabia can help limit Iran’s room to rebuild its influence there while working with Turkey, which already has substantial leverage in Syria.”

Although the Saudi-Syrian defense agreement demonstrates the extent to which Riyadh is committed to its bilateral partnership with Damascus, Magnier stressed that Syrian membership in the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement is a separate matter entirely.

“Saudi Arabia would gain a greater stake in the Levant, but it could also face a Syrian request for collective support after Israeli strikes,” he told RS. “Riyadh can advance its strategic interests in Syria through defense cooperation today. Extending a collective guarantee would require it to decide how much risk it is prepared to assume on the Israeli front.”

Where do Turkey and Pakistan stand?


Turkey is Syria’s “natural security partner,” said Watt, who pointed to two countries’ shared historic ties, Sunni identities, and common opposition to Kurdish separatism.

“Within the Agreement, Turkey stands out as having considerable military strength, and through NATO membership an important degree of strategic depth in facing down Israeli threats. In view of all this, the accession of Syria to the agreement seems merely a logical development,” he told RS.

“Israel has chosen to take an aggressive stance towards Turkey, but there is nothing inherent that prevents normal relations were Israel to reverse its expansionist policies in Lebanon, Syria and Palestine,” the former British diplomat added. “Turkey has maintained relations with Tehran in a way that facilitates the diplomatic solution sought by the Mecca Agreement.”

Meanwhile, Islamabad could gain from an enhanced diplomatic and military presence in the Middle East beyond the Gulf. However, Karim argues that “now there does not seem to be much excitement in Pakistan about” Islamabad acquiring “that kind of strategic and diplomatic influence” in Arab states outside the Gulf.

The risk of too many regional entanglements


For all the potential benefits, Syria’s efforts to balance regional relationships could become complicated if Damascus joins the pact. As Watt told RS, Syria’s membership would mark a departure from the neutrality pursued by post-Assad Syria, which could mean less diplomatic flexibility for Sharaa’s government moving forward.

For example, the rivalry between Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates raises real concerns about tensions between Damascus and Abu Dhabi resulting from Syrian membership. At the same time, Syria’s relationship with Iran would risk becoming more confrontational should Damascus enter the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement.

Ultimately, what remains to be seen is whether the pact’s collective-defense provisions will meaningfully enhance Syria’s security. As Turkey and Pakistan’s responses to Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia since the defense clause’s activation last month underscored, each Mecca Joint Defense Agreement signatory has its own national interests that stand to limit its willingness to become directly involved in conflicts involving its allies. This dynamic should cause officials in Damascus to question what concrete military commitments Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan will make when it comes to defending Syria from Israeli aggression.

America Invented the Drone War, So Why Is It Falling Behind?
item.description:
One mainstream document that called the United States’ sluggish reaction to this Revolution in Military Affairs (RMA) (and did so five years ago) was Christian Brose’s 2019 article in Foreign Affairs, “The New Revolution in Military Affairs: War’s Sci-Fi Future.” Brose’s bottom-line was the following: “Artificial intelligence, autonomous systems, ubiquitous sensors, advanced manufacturing, and quantum science will transform warfare as radically as the technologies that consumed Bloch [a nineteenth-century founder of the concept of RMAs]. And yet the U.S. government’s thinking about how to employ these new technologies is not keeping pace with their development.”

Editorial note: This is the second in a four-part series from former National Geospatial-Intelligence Director VADM Frank Whitworth (Ret.) on the reluctant revolution in military affairs and what it means for future intelligence and defense. This series of perspectives was adapted from a previous white paper written by the author two years ago, while he was on active duty.

Brose correctly identified a history of “change labels” in the last three decades with no resulting or substantial adjustment to core military methods. This trend began with the oncoming “military technical revolution” in 1992, moved to Admiral Arthur Cebrowski’s “Network-Centric Warfare” in the mid-1990s, Secretary Donald Rumsfeld’s “transformation” in the 9/11 era, and Deputy Secretary Robert Work’s “third offset strategy” in 2014. Each brought a slight twist on a common theme: “…emerging technologies will enable new battle networks of sensors and shooters to rapidly accelerate the process of detecting, targeting, and striking threats.”

Brose did not stop there. He was critical of American procurement choices over the last three decades as Washington “…poured money into newer versions of old military platforms and prayed for technological miracles to come (which often became acquisition debacles when those miracles did not materialize.” Brose was prescient in identifying how inexpensive uncrewing could be – and how much change it required of the military mindset. Well before Replicator (DOD’s primary development program for autonomous vehicles) became a glimmer in anyone’s eye, Brose identified the need for fleets of drones, with ubiquitous communications and elements of autonomy.

To reiterate, this paper does not intend to prove and explain the United States’ reluctant acceptance of every facet of this “drones, codes, and spacecraft” RMA. In fact, during our application of Marshall’s principles, we cited three major developments that help rule-out our reluctance to accept non-proximate warfare in the space and cyber domains: specifically, the establishment of the United States Space Force, USPACECOM, and USCYBERCOM. Drones are a different matter, though – and to prove our reluctance, we will (a) compare the United States’ rate of “military drone fleet” development to that of Ukraine, and (b) demonstrate the stark difference in DOD’s acquisition budgets between manned and unmanned assets.

Globally, the number of nations with armed drone programs has accelerated. The rapid growth of armed, medium altitude, long endurance (MALE) drones (such as the MQ-9 Reaper) since 2001 is evident in this graphic from Drone Wars UK:

Source: Drone Wars UK

These large, MALE drones are important because they can deliver munitions lengthy distances and damage strategic targets such as infrastructure and headquarters. Since Russia’s invasion in 2022, Ukraine has transformed itself into a world leader of drone technology and employment. In fact, Ukrainian President Zelensky just announced in December 2024 that his country will produce 30,000 MALE drones next year. That nearly triples DOD’s entire drone fleet of 11,000 (a number that even includes smaller, non-MALE assets such as the hand-launched RQ-11B Raven). The United States’ production of military drones has been lapped numerically by Ukraine in only two years—despite America’s 20-year head-start in developing the technology.

The Ukrainian Ministry of Defense Transformation reports seven drone models were produced domestically in 2022, and that number has grown tenfold to 67 in only two years. Similarly, Ukraine now has an astounding 200 domestic drone manufacturers. This stands in stark contrast to America’s drone manufacturing sector, which has declined. With the United States’ withdrawal from Afghanistan and a reduction in military contracts, IBIS World estimates the United States has only 73 businesses in the UAV manufacturing sector. As representationally depicted in Figure 3, the sector is declining at a Compound Annual Growth Rate (CAGR) of 5.8 percent to $4.0 billion through 2024 (dropping 21.4 percent this year alone.)

UAV Manufacturing in the U.S. — Source: IBISWorld

In examining expenditures reported in the Office of the Under Secretary of Defense, Comptroller’s April 4, 2024 report, “Program Acquisition Cost by Weapon System, FY2025,” the United States’ reluctance to adopting the “drones” portion of this RMA is demonstrated further. As depicted in Figure 4, unmanned aircraft systems account for less than four percent of DOD’s expenditures dedicated to overall aviation and related systems. Separately, there are no “unmanned” wedges in either the $48 billion of proposed expenditures for shipbuilding and maritime systems or the $13 billion or proposed expenditures for ground systems.
