item.title: Where Did the Billions From Venezuela's Oil Go?
item.description:
“We've won Venezuela and [have] taken out billions and billions and billions of dollars already. And we will be taking out many billions of dollars and get along very well. And -- you could call it a territory, you could call it whatever you want. We won that war in less than one hour.”

That was President Trump during his telecast 60 Minutes interview on CBS with Ross Douthat on November 8. However, CBS also has released the transcript of the entire, unedited transcript of the 51-minute interview during which Trump also said, but was not part of the telecast version, “Venezuela, where, by the way, we’ve taken out 50 times what the war has cost already. To the victor belong the spoils.”

I bring up those remarks because last August I wrote a column questioning what had happened to those billions of dollars from Venezuelan oil that Trump referred to many times earlier than the 60 Minutes interview – in fact, Trump began less than a week after the U.S. military seized then-Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife on January 3, 2026, and, in effect, took over that country.

Douthat did not ask Trump anything more about the “billions and billions” in the 60 Minutes interview – I wish he had.

Also not discussed was what Trump last August 28 on Truth Social called, “THE BIGGEST OIL DEAL IN WORLD HISTORY!” where the U.S., through a Pentagon agency, has become the 35 percent owner of what a White House fact sheet called, “the second-largest private oil company by [Venezuelan oil] reserves in the world.”

I will discuss the many still secret parts of that Trump administration deal below.

But the public release last week by the State Department of the American accounting firm KPMG LLP’s 53-page Report on Venezuela Custody Account Operations January - September 2026 October 29, 2026 also failed to answer questions that I and others have raised about what happened to those initial “billions” from Venezuelan oil.

For example, during his January 9, 2026, meeting with oil company leaders at the White House, Trump told the press that was present that Venezuela had already given the U.S. 30 million barrels of what had been previously-sanctioned oil that it had on hand.

“That's about $4 billion worth,” Trump announced back in January, adding, “And it's on our way to the United States right now. And we want to thank Venezuela for that. And we're working very well with them [Acting President Delcy Rodriguez and her government], obviously, or they wouldn't have been so generous.”

At that January 9, meeting, Trump also announced his Executive Order, Safeguarding Venezuelan Oil Revenue for the Good of the American and Venezuelan People under which Venezuelan oil revenues were to be held in a Venezuela Custody Account (VCA) set up by the U.S. Treasury. The VCA was initially based in a Qatar bank, but moved to Citibank in New York in late January. Distribution of the funds for use by the Venezuelan government would be determined by the Secretary of State.

Last week’s KPMG report showed that VCA in January received $500 million. On January 28, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told the Senate Foreign Relations Committee the payment of $300 million had already been made from the VCA “to keep [Venezuelan] sanitation workers, police officers, government workers on staff,” and that it was from Venezuelan oil sales totaling $500 million.

The KPMG report also showed the VCA received $1 billion in February, another $1.5 billion, and another $2.1 billion in April.

On April 16, the State Department’s Michael Kozak, a senior official from the Bureau of Western Hemisphere Affairs, in testimony before the House Foreign Affairs Western Hemisphere Subcommittee, disclosed “around $3 billion” of Venezuelan oil revenue had moved through the VCA “paying the salaries of government workers in Venezuela; buying supplies for their oil industry, and so on, other things that benefit the public.”

Since it appears that the VCA did not receive as much as $4 billion until April, that again raises the question what happened to the $4 billion in Venezuelan oil Trump said was “on the way” to the U.S. in early January.

Overall, The KPMG report showed that between January and September 30, 2026, the VCA received $12.26 billion from sales primarily of Venezuelan crude oil and petroleum transactions, with minor amounts from gold, minerals, and fertilizer. In turn, following review and approval by the State Department and Treasury, some $12.11 billion has gone to the Venezuelan central bank or directly to vendors.

As mentioned above, another flow of Venezuelan oil money to the U.S. is coming from the most unusual “historic oil agreement” Trump announced built around the interim Venezuelan government granting what a White House August 31 fact sheet said was “100-year concessions for 17 oil fields with proven reserves of approximately 65 billion barrels” to a company named North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP).

I should point out any 100 year oil concession violates Venezuelan law.

According to a September 2, White House fact sheet, the 17 oil fields were “previously controlled or operated by Russian and Chinese firms, or by corrupt cronies of Maduro and Chavez.”

More important was that the Trump administration signed a joint agreement with NABEP’s parent company, based in Barbados, that grants the U.S. government a 35%-stake in ownership in that corporate parent and the right to buy 20% of NABEP’s Venezuelan oil output at production cost.

Here is the way the September 2, White House fact sheet described that deal. It said the joint agreement “was signed by Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth,” and “at no cost to the American taxpayer, NABEP has granted the U.S. Department of War’s Office of Strategic Capital a 35% equity stake in its corporate parent, representing up to hundreds of billions in value and dividends for the United States.”

In addition, the White House release said, “NABEP has granted the U.S. Department of State the right to purchase, at production cost, a guaranteed 20% of the off-take from all current and future fields NABEP will operate.”

That means that a Pentagon agency is the over one-third owner of a major Venezuelan oil company and the State Department may be the substantial buyer of the oil output of that company. In short, two departments of the U.S. government are now in the oil business.

The September White House release made the further points that, “This is a deal with a private company – not the Venezuelan interim government. It’s not a deal with the interim

In an October 20, report, ProPublica, which said its staff had “reviewed a copy of the 18-page strategic partnership agreement signed for the United States by Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth,” points out, “The deal document provides little information about the owners and investors behind the parent [Barbados] company, who could receive enormous wealth from the arrangement.”

In short, the public ought to know who are the new business partners of the U.S. Government?

ProPublica also questioned NABEP’s chief executive, Alejandro Betancourt, whom it describes as “a globe-trotting Venezuelan oligarch who has faced money-laundering investigations in three countries.”

The agreement gives the U.S. government veto power over the appointment of any member of NABEP’s seven-member board of directors and a majority must be U.S. citizens. ProPublica says the board members have 15-year terms, a move it was told “designed to prevent future U.S. and Venezuelan leaders from dismantling the enterprise.” Betancourt is the only board member named by the agreement.

According to ProPublica, “The signed agreement is marked as a ‘sensitive’ government document. That classification is commonly used to shield a variety of federal records from public release, including those containing personnel information, details about ongoing law enforcement operations and matters protected by attorney-client privilege. The document also contains a confidentiality clause barring Betancourt’s company from disclosing the ‘existence and terms” of the U.S. government agreement.”

Hopefully, the incoming Democratic-controlled Congress will include the Venezuelan oil deal in one of its investigations.

Meanwhile, on October 27, Trump diverted from a campaign appearance in Texas to make a statement that day pier-side in Corpus Christi, along with Rubio, where two tankers carrying one million barrels of Venezuelan crude produced by NABEP had arrived.

Betancourt was on hand to say, “This first shipment since the U.S.-NABEP deal will be followed by thousands of such arrivals, and each one shows the world that Venezuela is back as a dependable energy supplier, with the United States as its anchor buyer.”

Trump told the press, “We took over Venezuela very successfully and they've sent me as a gift a boatload of a million barrels of oil and I'm giving that to the United States.”

Three days later, Reuters reported, “NABEP initially said the oil was delivered under Washington's right to buy a portion of the company's production at cost. It later said it gave the shipment to the U.S. at no cost to U.S. taxpayer ‘to recognize the historic nature of the agreement.’"

This is an oil agreement worth following.

item.title: The Philippines did not deliver a South China Sea Code of Conduct. But it has shown what ASEAN can achieve
item.description:
The Philippines did not deliver a South China Sea Code of Conduct. But it has shown what ASEAN can achieve Expert comment jon.wallace 17 November 2026

This week’s summit did not produce the Code many desire. But as ASEAN Chair Manila has laid a useful foundation for the Code, while making important progress on regional connectivity.

When it assumed the Chair of ASEAN last year, the Philippines placed negotiations to establish a South China Sea Code of Conduct (COC) at the centre of its agenda. An agreement has been desired for decades, to help reduce territorial and other tensions between China and regional countries. The need for the COC is clear: Philippine ships have continued to clash with Chinese Coast Guard vessels throughout the year, around disputed areas such as Scarborough Shoal. 

But Philippines Foreign Affairs Secretary Theresa Lazaro cooled expectations of an agreement at this week’s ASEAN summit. In a recent statement, she said that while around 80 per cent of the provisions are agreed, ‘sticking points’ still remain. It is therefore unlikely to be concluded by the end of the year with Philippines as ASEAN Chair.

But the Philippines tenure has been about more than just the COC. In a region of diverging priorities, security alignments, and threat perceptions, Manila should be judged by how far it has boosted ASEAN’s utility as an independent diplomatic actor able to strengthen regional solidarity.

Progress under pressure

The role of ASEAN Chair was clearly going to test the Philippines: How would it reconcile its national security interests with its responsibilities as the leader of a forum for regional cooperation? And would Beijing see Manila as a good faith actor on the COC?

The Philippines is, after all, one of the oldest treaty partners of the US. Those ties are getting stronger under President Ferdinand ‘Bongbong’ Marcos, while its relationship with China becomes ever more fractious – a stance not shared by all ASEAN partners. 

Beside these obvious impediments, the overlapping and complex nature of the claims in South China Sea waters made the COC a tricky subject to negotiate within the bloc, let alone with China. But under the stewardship of the Philippines delegations met every month this year and have managed to produce a substantial part of an agreement – a significant jump after two decades of diplomatic deadlock. 

There is no official confirmation on what the sticking points were, but past statements suggest issues around legal implementation, geographical scope, and terms of reference prevented a final agreement. Singapore, next year’s chair, enjoys a more stable relationship with Beijing and may stand a better chance of ironing out these final elements. Even this remains uncertain, but setting up Singapore with the best possible chance always looked like the most realistic ambition for the Philippines on the COC, and it has made good progress to that end. 

Outside of COC negotiations, the Philippines has managed to make significant moves on some other stated priorities. The Philippines assumed the Chair of ASEAN under the theme ‘Navigating our future, together’. This focussed on three core pillars: Peace and security anchors, prosperity corridors, and people empowerment. 

To this end, Manila concluded negotiations of the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA). This is the world’s first binding region-wide digital economy deal, which will better integrate the region and foster greater cross-border data flows and end-to-end digital trade, promising to bring in $2 trillion by 2030. 

The Philippines also championed the ASEAN Leaders’ Declaration on Strategic Trade Management, which aims to establish unified frameworks to strengthen the resilience of regional supply chains. 

And it established the ASEAN Centre of Excellence for Creative Industries, fostering a more interconnected creative economy and greater cultural exchange. Manila has also pushed for greater collaboration on disaster preparedness, with a focus on pooling resources in the face of natural calamities.

One significant area where little has been achieved is the crisis in Myanmar: diplomatic progress on the issue was a strategic and symbolic challenge for the Philippines and ASEAN’s credibility as a peace-making body. In the end, ASEAN’s agenda remains stalled. The summit agreed to pursue ‘calibrated engagement’ in pursuit of ASEAN’s ‘5 Point Consensus’, and leaves the door open for gradual restoration to the bloc. But as a unified group, ASEAN appears to have little hope of influencing Myanmar’s military government.

Successful summitry 

This summit needed to go well for President Marcos. The Philippines has been pursuing its ASEAN agenda at a time of mounting domestic pressure. The war in Iran has strained energy supply chains, hindering access to necessities. Summer saw massive losses from tsunamis and earthquakes, and impeachment proceedings against the Vice President. The Marcos administration received its lowest ever approval ratings this month, as protestors clashed with police on the eve of the summit. 

Want to hear more on the future of global trade?

Join us at our Global Trade Conference for expert analysis on the shifting rules of the global economy.

The event was ostensibly been productive. More than 150 outcome documents were reviewed and approved. A new ASEAN free trade agreement has been agreed with Canada. Brazil and Canada have committed $540 million for rainforest protection. And the event presented a significant opportunity for the bloc to interact with influential leaders including President Donald Trump, Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Prime Minister Mark Carney, and President Lula da Silva.

And as always at summits, meetings on the sidelines provided opportunities for important diplomacy: Japan’s PM Takaichi and South Korea’s President Lee Jae Myung held their fourth bilateral meeting. And the Quad convened for the first time in two years. 

But ASEAN countries must see real returns from these convenings to be considered a success. And it is imperative that ASEAN as a unit is seen as a key player rather than a platform through which bilateral deals can be done. Indeed, Philippines President Marcos emphasized a ‘whole-of-ASEAN approach’ in his plenary speech.

This focus on unifying regional interests is not for the sake of ASEAN alone, but part of a wider strategy to protect the Philippines in the face of broader geopolitical trends. The test will be if Manila can carry this sentiment forward beyond its tenure as chair – something that may prove difficult.

Preparing for the storms ahead

2027 will see Singapore become ASEAN Chair with the organization set to be tested by deepening faultlines on AI alliances, critical mineral exploration, and supply chain and energy resilience. 

Divergences are already appearing among members on how best to approach these issues. Coming on top of existing territorial disputes, strained relations within the bloc seem likely. However, even if ASEAN countries have diverging interests, they will never be able to escape the reality of what they share: geography and history. 

As the overlapping threats of climate change, great power rivalry, and an unstable global economy demand a cohesive regional response, the Philippines’ priorities of cohesion and greater interdependence will be key to the region’s survival. What this year has made clear is that grand international dealmaking of the kind represented by the COC may continue to prove difficult for the group. Despite this, ASEAN can provide an indispensable function, facilitating interoperability and integration that fuels growth and secures sovereignty. 

As President Marcos said at the summit’s opening, the coming years will be about ‘not only where ASEAN is headed, but what ASEAN must become’. For years the ASEAN has been dismissed as ineffectual and underperforming. But the group has endured. And the Philippines period as Chair has perhaps shown the bloc’s true value – driving incremental but unyielding change towards an increasingly interconnected region.

JERUSALEM, Nov 17 (Reuters) - Israel's parliament voted on Tuesday to select a new speaker opposed to the agenda of Benjamin Netanyahu, a potential first step in rolling back theprime minister's divisive political agenda even as his main rival struggles to form a government.

Parties led by Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu's main competitor in an inconclusive October election, voted to install Matan Kahana, a member of Eisenkot's centre-right Yashar party, with 66 voting in favor of Kahana and 52 voting for another candidate, according to the office of the spokesperson for the parliament.

item.title: Israel parliament elects Eisenkot ally as speaker in blow for Netanyahu
item.description:
Israeli lawmakers on Tuesday elected a parliament speaker from the camp opposed to caretaker prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, a first step towards rolling back the legacy of the country's divisive veteran leader.

Sixty six lawmakers out of 120 voted in favour of Matan Kahana, an ally of former military chief Gadi Eisenkot who has until next month to form a government to replace Netanyahu.

Netanyahu's Likud party had put forward Ofir Katz as its own candidate, who received 52 votes.

item.title: Norm Coleman: Hegseth adviser double-dipping for Israel, Saudi
item.description:
This article was co-published with The Guardian

One of defense secretary Pete Hegseth’s key advisers faces questions about potential conflicts of interest over his many roles, including advising the US defense department, Saudi Arabia, and an Israeli defense contractor.

Former Republican senator Norm Coleman emerged as an informal yet omnipresent guide for Hegseth in December 2024 as the former Fox News host navigated confirmation hearings for his nomination as defense secretary. Hegseth now finds himself under fire after articles of impeachment were filed by Republican congressman Thomas Massie charging him with “high crimes and misdemeanors,” including waging war against Iran in violation of the War Powers Act, but Hegseth’s imprint on the Pentagon goes beyond the disastrous war against Iran.

At the start of his marathon 4 hours and 24 minutes hearing before the Senate armed services committee — a hearing that delved into allegations of sexual misconduct, workplace drinking and marital infidelity — Hegseth took time to “thank the former senator from Minnesota, Norm Coleman, for his mentorship and friendship in this process”

Coleman’s service to Hegseth appears to have been rewarded in June, when the secretary of war appointed Coleman to the Defense Policy Board, uniquely situating Coleman to advise on defense procurement decisions of interest to the former senator’s clients.

“Serving as a sherpa to rich people seeking to climb Mount Everest is dangerous and thankless work that is often underappreciated by Westerners,” said Jeff Hauser, founder and executive director of the Revolving Door Project, a group that scrutinizes executive branch appointees to ensure they use their office to serve the broad public interest. “But serving successfully as a sherpa to a controversial nominee tends to breed enormous goodwill.”

Coleman is a man of many, often highly remunerative, hats. He is the chairman of the Republican Jewish Coalition (RJC), a group comprised of a who’s-who of pro-Israel Republican megadonors. He chairs the Congressional Leadership Fund, one of the biggest super Pacs supporting House Republicans. And he serves as a lobbyist for Saudi Arabia and now as vice chairman of the Defense Policy Board, a Pentagon advisory committee focusing on “matters pertaining to strategic planning, the policy implications of U.S. force structure and modernization, regional defense policies, and other defense policy and national security issues of special interest to the Department”.

Last year, Coleman added another job to his resume: senior adviser to Kinetica, an Israeli weapons company ideally positioned to profit from deeper integration between the US and Israeli weapons development industries, posing a potential conflict of interest for Coleman as he advises the Pentagon and Republican candidates on matters related to the defense budget and weapons procurement.

“Norm Coleman is a walking conflict of interest on the Pentagon Defense Policy Board,” said Craig Holman, a government affairs lobbyist at Public Citizen, a consumer advocacy organization that opposes corporate influence in government. “Most other advisory boards will not allow the appointment of registered lobbyists.”

It is not illegal to simultaneously work as a lobbyist and advise the Pentagon.

Questions about the national security implications of US-Israeli defense integration came to a head earlier this year with the introduction of Section 219 of the House National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), legislation that would more deeply intertwine the U.S. and Israeli militaries and commit the U.S. to bilateral research and development and co-production of weapons, joint ventures and licensing agreements.

Mark Dubowitz, CEO of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies (FDD), a group whose mission includes “provid[ing] education to enhance Israel’s image in North America,” explained that intertwining the U.S. and Israeli militaries and weapons development systems is a necessary step in the face of polling showing rapidly diminishing support for Israel among Americans of all political stripes. “Those figures should concern Israel and its friends because, ultimately, public opinion shapes policy,” said Dubowitz, writing in Israel Hayom, an outlet owned by pro-Israel megadonor Miriam Adelson, last month.

Dubowitz went on to advise: “Most importantly, Israel and the United States should deepen their military, technological, intelligence and economic integration to such an extent that inflicting financial harm on Israel would also carry a significant cost for Washington.”

FDD, which endorsed congressional efforts to mandate U.S.-Israel defense integration, has a unique tie to Coleman’s Israeli client: its board member Isaac Applbaum is chairman of Kinetica. And Kinetica claims it is uniquely situated to benefit from such an intertwining of the U.S. defense sector with Israel.

Kinetica reported in February that Coleman, speaking in his capacity as an adviser to the company at a conference in Tel Aviv, “shared his perspective from his deep proximity to the U.S. defense establishment.”

“He highlighted that the U.S. Department of Defense is actively seeking new technologies to integrate into its systems – a shift from a landscape once dominated exclusively by large defense primes to one that is increasingly open to emerging innovation,” wrote Kinetica on LinkedIn. “For Israel, as a strategic U.S. ally, this represents a significant opportunity to scale into the American defense ecosystem.”

Speaking to the Defense Brief in June, Kinetica founding partner Aaron Applbaum (Isaac’s son), reiterated this sentiment, explaining the business strategy behind the Israeli startup in a broader ecosystem of growing military spending in the U.S., NATO, Japan, and the Middle East. “It’s a generational opportunity to start a new platform,” said Applbaum.

In a LinkedIn post later that month, the company cheered its bet on Coleman as a validation of its business strategy, celebrating his appointment as VP of the Defense Policy Board, writing:

“Congratulations to Kinetica’s Senior Advisor, Senator Norm Coleman, on his appointment as Vice Chair of the Defense Policy Board, which advises the U.S. Secretary of Defense and senior Pentagon officials on strategic and national security issues.

“As an advisor to Kinetica, Senator Coleman brings a rare combination of policy, leadership, foreign affairs experience and a deep understanding of the U.S.-Israel strategic relationship.

His appointment reflects an important part of the Kinetica thesis – defense policy, technological superiority and allied innovation are no longer separate conversations. They are part of the same national security mission.”

Coleman’s exact role with Kinetica is unclear, but his work for other weapons manufacturers and contractors reveals Pentagon lobbying efforts in the months leading up to his appointment to the Defense Policy Board, raising questions about potential conflicts of interest.

“Human beings cannot actually firewall parts of their brain from each other, which means that it is impossible for one’s work for the United States to fail to influence one’s work for Saudi Arabia or defense companies — and vice versa,” said Hauser. “The difference is that Saudi Arabia and defense contractors want their paid agents to have multiple loyalties so that they can be more effective in return for cash, whereas the U.S. government ought to reasonably expect for the undivided loyalty of those who serve it.”

In his capacity as senior counsel at legal giant Hogan Lovells Cadwalader, Coleman served as a lobbyist on the firm’s account for Hidden Level Inc., a company producing drone detection systems. The firm’s work included outreach to the departments of defense and homeland security and the White House as part of efforts “regarding drone airspace management and security capabilities”, according to lobbying disclosure filings.

Coleman also helped in “raising the profile” of the SkyWater Technology foundry “as a trusted domestic semiconductor manufacturer,” according to the lobbying firm’s description of its work lobbying various Washington agencies, including the Pentagon, on behalf of Coretsu, an AI and technology company seeking to promote “technology applications for legal and regulatory analysis.”

After his appointment to the Defense Policy Board, Coleman continued to be listed on the firm’s lobbying disclosures, revealing he was a lobbyist on at least one account that lobbied the Department of Defense: Bear SVTP Development LLC. The company retained Coleman and two other lobbyists to assist with issues related to “[l]and development with respect to AI Data Centers and federal regulation,” according to lobbying disclosures.

“It’s a very suspect situation that Norm Coleman is manipulating: he’s advising the Pentagon on what policies to do while he’s also advising contractors on what to do,” said Holman. “But it doesn’t seem to be illegal, just self-serving and unethical.”

“The Federal Advisory Committee Act just bans individual lobbyists, not those who serve as lobbyists for another firm like Hogan Lovell,” said Holman, referring to legislation dictating the operations of advisory committees like the Defense Policy Board.

Members of the Defense Policy Board seemingly holding significant conflicts of interest is not a new or unusual occurrence. A Center for Public Integrity investigation in 2003 found that nine out of thirty members of the Board had ties to contractors with more than $76 billion in Pentagon contracts and four were registered lobbyists, including its chairman, Richard Perle, who had just resigned his chairmanship. Perle drew fire for his business relationship with Global Crossing Ltd and satellite maker Loral Space & Communications Ltd, but a heavily redacted report by the Pentagon inspector general concluded that he did not violate any ethics laws.

Lobbyists face greater scrutiny after the Republicans’ midterms debacle. Stephen Miller, Trump’s new chief of staff, issued a memo ordering White House staffers to get approval before meeting lobbyists.

Coleman, Hogan Lovells Cadwalader and Kinetica did not respond to requests for comment.

item.title: See the damage to the Crimean Bridge after Ukraine’s strikes: New video filmed from a passing train reveals a massive gap in the roadway
item.description: On the morning of November 18, a video began circulating on social media showing footage of a destroyed span of the Crimean Bridge after strikes by the Ukrainian military. The Ukrainian monitoring Telegram channel Exilenova+ published the footage, filmed from a train traveling along the railway section of the bridge, which runs parallel to the roadway. The train takes almost 30 seconds to pass the gap left where the span once stood. Ukraine struck the bridge on two consecutive nights, November 16 and 17. After the first attack, the Kremlin said the damage was “minor”; after the second, Russian presidential spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said the bridge would be rebuilt and would be “even better than before.” Volodymyr Zelensky called the attack on the Crimean Bridge an “unprecedented operation” that had been in preparation for several weeks. The last strike on the bridge, according to Zelensky, was carried out with Neptune, Flamingo, and Ruta missiles.

item.title: Yalta this is not: The Xi–Trump–Putin meeting is China’s show and America’s loss
item.description:
Yalta this is not: The Xi–Trump–Putin meeting is China’s show and America’s loss Expert comment jon.wallace 18 November 2026

The meeting offers little for US interests, risk for Ukraine – and a sobering image for Europe and other countries. 

President Xi Jinping, President Donald Trump and President Vladimir Putin might be tempted to accept the comparisons being drawn between their coming talks in Shenzhen on Thursday and the Yalta summit of 1945. There, US President Franklin Delano Roosevelt, UK Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet Premier Joseph Stalin set out the post-war peace, carving up the world between them – though the end of the British Empire was already inevitable. 

But this week’s meeting is no Yalta. It is showmanship. Any deals to be done are small – and they are all in China’s favour, unless Trump decides to side with Russia over Ukraine. 

For the rest of the world, particularly the UK and European Union, the display is a reminder of the urgent need to shore up regional alliances, the United Nations, and the rule of international law where possible. 

The players

Trump has most to lose from going to this summit. The US would have been better off had he not gone. Perhaps he was attracted by the image of standing shoulder to shoulder with two authoritarian leaders he seems to admire – more than he does the leaders of the US’s democratic allies. Perhaps it was the possibility of taking part in a Yalta-like exercise in shaping the world. 

If that was his judgement, it is wrong. For a start, unlike the Yalta photograph of 1945 (where the three leaders were seated, concealing the fact that the ailing Roosevelt needed a wheelchair) the US president will not be placed in the centre. That role will go to Xi, as host. But that positioning will also reflect the reality. Xi is the leader of the power with the least need of concessions from the others. 

Besides matters of presentation, by attending this meeting Trump surrenders yet again what has been since 1945 the US’s strongest card: that it has been the ‘leader of the free world’, upholding the rights of democracies and acting as a beacon to all those who espouse those principles. Instead, Trump carries the banner of ‘Might Makes Right’ to the summit. 

Unlike Trump, Putin has much to gain from this meeting. Russia is no superpower. Its economy is dwindling, with 40 per cent of production diverted to his war in Ukraine. With this summit in mind, Ukraine this week bombed Putin’s prized Kerch bridge to Crimea, built in 2014 after Russia’s invasion of the peninsula. The main span lies in rubble, blocking maritime traffic and the resupply of Russian troops fighting Ukraine. 

But standing with Xi and Trump, Putin will look like one of the three main leaders of the world, not the instigator of a war which has cost Russia almost half a million military dead, according to reports – with no end in sight.

The stakes

President Trump is a supplicant at this meeting – to the point where it is dangerous for him to enter into negotiations. He wants to talk about curbing the growth or renewal of nuclear weapons arsenals, partly with a view to bringing down cost. But China has said from the beginning this is a non-starter, given that its nuclear arsenal is far behind those of the other two. 

Trump may also want to push China on critical minerals: he has accused Beijing of not making good on the deal struck a year ago in South Korea. But as then, when he threatened tariffs only to swiftly back down when Xi threatened to withhold minerals supplies, he will find he has a weak hand.

He will be similarly on the back foot if Xi presses him to ensure the continued supply of top US chips from Nvidia, whether legally exported or through intermediaries. The defenestration of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO over a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy complicates the picture. But the fact remains, despite the weight of opinion in Congress and the opposition of Trump’s top team, Trump, Huang and commerce secretary Howard Lutnick have facilitated the chip trade with China. Should Trump try to change direction, it would not be surprising if Xi threatened to turn off minerals supply once again. 

The wars in Ukraine and Iran are not likely to get useful attention from the trio. China has no incentive to get involved in Iran, a war of Trump’s making from which he is trying to extricate the US. And Beijing is quietly stirring the conflict in Ukraine, helping Russia by buying its oil and selling it engines and components used in aerial warfare. Having Europe preoccupied with the conflict suits China fine. 

The danger for Ukraine is that Trump uses this summit to try to advance his notion of peace, including giving Russia territory it has not managed to seize by force. It is striking that Ukraine made a point of saying that its strike on Kerch bridge was conducted without Starlink, Elon Musk’s satellite communication system, which it accuses the US of turning off or switching to slower speeds to put pressure on Kyiv. 

Ukraine will be able to hold out, but only with European help. There is bitterness among Ukrainian officials that despite the heavy rebuff to Trump in the US mid-term elections, a Democrat-dominated Congress – while talking tougher on Putin – is unlikely to send more funds Ukraine’s way.

Europe, not present at this summit, is in the crosshairs of all three leaders. Trump remains in open dispute with European leaders over their dependency on US defence and alleged cultural decline. China is unhappy about the tariffs the EU is now considering, targeting its exports. And Russia is of course probing European unity over Ukraine. 

European leaders, including the UK, need to look hard at this trio and work out their response on security and trade. They have every incentive to work out a common front: a live war is taking place on their eastern flank, as their main security guarantor becomes increasingly unpredictable. And technological competition from China threatens to annihilate their manufacturing industries. 

Other countries will look at the same photograph and similarly count their friends and new alliances. The smaller the country, the more it needs the rule of international law and respect for international institutions. 

Xi, Trump and Putin may gather believing they dominate the world. But their meeting gives others every reason to look for ways to stand together.

item.title: Tom Friedman’s deceptive effort to lure Dems to escalate in Iran
item.description:
The centrist Democrats’ campaign to rescue - not end - Donald Trump’s illegal war with Iran has officially begun. Behold Tom Friedman’s column today in The New York Times.

Tom puts forward an argument with a clever structure. He starts by blasting Trump’s decision to start the war. He cites numerous data points, including testimony from GCC officials that tears massive holes in the White House’s narrative that the situation is under control, that Iran is on the ropes, and that Trump has won the battle for the Strait of Hormuz.

This paragraph, for instance:

“I had a briefing from a senior Emirati oil official who shared with me a digital map of the relentless Iranian attacks on the fleet of Emirati-owned oil tankers — not when they pass through the Strait of Hormuz near Iran, but when they try to transit the Persian Gulf in Emirati waters, hugging the country’s eastern coastline. These are highly sophisticated attacks, mostly with cruise missiles and drones, that go right into the oil tankers’ engine rooms and disable them. Bull’s-eye every time. The Emirates then has to send tugboats out to rescue the crews and pull the disabled tankers into port. This is happening almost every day.”

Now add the testimony from the head of the U.S. Navy, who revealed that insuring ships through the Strait of Hormuz has skyrocketed from $54,000 to a staggering $64 million. That’s a jaw-dropping 118,418 percent increase, a devastating indictment of just how unsustainable and ruinous Trump’s so-called control over the Strait has become. Having brought readers along with him, particularly centrist Democratic leaders in Congress whom this piece specifically targets, Tom takes a dark and sudden turn.

Rather than urging Democrats to help end the war, he pivots to arguing against cutting its funding, relying on arguments so flimsy and absurd they almost defy belief. Take this paragraph, for example:

“I think it would be a mistake for Democrats to try to cut off funding for the war, just as I thought it was a mistake to talk about defunding the police. You defund it, you own it. That is, Trump will say forevermore that he had the Iranians on the ropes and then the Democrats pulled the rug out from under him. Democrats should do nothing to weaken U.S. leverage on the Iranians. It is a sick regime and a truly destabilizing, malign actor in the region and around the world, one that is now providing Russians with the advanced drone technology that Moscow is using to destroy Ukraine’s energy infrastructure before winter.”

So in Tom’s upside-down logic, if Democrats defund the war, they own it, but if they keep funding it, somehow Trump still owns it. Reality, of course, is the reverse. If Democrats choose to bankroll an illegal war their voters have demanded they end, they become complicit, sharing the dubious distinction of co-ownership with Trump and Israel. As I’ve pointed out on this Substack, with shifting voting patterns—especially among younger voters—Democrats are setting themselves up for a reckoning in 2028 if they rescue the war instead of ending it.

This is a stunningly moronic argument Tom puts forward, but admittedly, it will resonate with centrist Democrats who have secretly supported the war all along.

Tom is correct, however, that Trump will falsely claim that he was about to win the war but that the Democrats “pulled the rug out from under him,” to which I respond: Who cares??

Should Democrats really keep an illegal, losing war alive just to stop Trump from spinning another feeble lie? Is this the leadership voters crave—turning a blind eye to an illegal war and the affordability crisis it fuels, all to obsess over Trump’s endless lying?

The American people can endure Trump’s lies. We live with them every day. What Americans cannot live with is a war that makes actual living an increasingly difficult proposition. A war that weakens the US on every front and that destabilizes the global economy to the point of a potential depression. But Tom believes Democrats should be more concerned about Trump adding one more lie to his repertoire.

Then Tom adds the ever-present false-choice argument that Washington’s foreign policy establishment obsesses over: If you do X, enemy Y will become stronger.

So defunding the war will make Iran stronger, Tom says, even though he admits that it is the war itself that has put Iran in a stronger position. So the Democrats should continue a losing war out of fear that ending the war will make the US lose even further. The Israeli officials who pushed Trump into this war in the first place could not have put it better.

But this sentence reveals the logical conclusion of Tom’s argument. In reality, he is not arguing for a mere continuation of the war. He wants the Democrats to escalate the war. Because, according to Tom’s own assessment, continuing the war will not change the picture: The US will lose more, regional countries will pay a high price, and Iran’s position will be strengthened.

The only way to reverse Iran’s gains, the implicit logic reads, is to escalate the war in order to press Iran back. This is the option the Israelis are pushing for. This is the option Trump is considering.

And this is the option Tom is deceptively luring Democrats into enabling.

This article was republished from Trita Parsi's Substack

item.title: The Guardian view on the Trump, Xi and Putin meeting: it may be a first, but it’s not progress | Editorial
item.description:
A trilateral gathering is good news for China and Russia, but bad for the US – and its traditional allies

“Historic” is a neutral descriptor, not a favourable one. Things can be unprecedented for good reason. Donald Trump’s meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China on Thursday will be the first time that the leaders of the US, China and Russia have gathered for talks as a trio. The trilateral on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is striking, but it is not an achievement.

The lack of a clear agenda is telling: the spectacle really is the substance. Mr Trump sees international affairs in terms of spheres of influence. This meeting reinforces the obvious conclusion for the rest of the world – that they don’t get to sit at the table, only to be on the plate. Mr Xi promotes the notion of a multipolar world. Others would be more sympathetic if all three governments were not determinedly undermining multilateralism.
